target.title: Large-Scale Visual Speech Recognition
target.version: v3 (dated 1 Oct 2018 on the first page)

read.pdf: No PDF supplied; read the text-extracted captions for Figs. 1–10, Tables 1–5, appendices A–F, and the complete reference list

entries.text: The authors claim a novel method for large-vocabulary continuous visual speech recognition and substantial WER reductions over prior methods.
entries.condition: The claim concerns continuous, open-vocabulary visual speech recognition.
entries.quote: In this paper, we contribute a novel method for large-vocabulary continuous visual speech recognition.

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first combination of deep phoneme recognition with production-grade word-level decoding.
entries.condition: V2P predicts phoneme distributions; a separate decoder produces word sequences.
entries.quote: Our approach is the ﬁrst to combine a deep learning-based phoneme recognition model with production-grade word-level decoding techniques.

entries.text: The separate lexicon and language model are claimed to let users change vocabulary without retraining the phoneme network.
entries.condition: The claim follows from separating phoneme prediction from the lexicon and LM in the decoder.
entries.quote: This ﬂexible design enables us to easily accommodate very large vocabularies, and in fact we can extend the size of the vocabulary without having to retrain the deep network.

entries.text: LSVSR is reported as 2,934,899 utterances, 3,886 hours, and a 127,055-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: YouTube-derived English sentence-level audio-video-text corpus; Table 1 compares visual speech datasets.

entries.text: The authors claim LSVSR has a 2.2× larger vocabulary than the next-largest comparison.
entries.condition: Authors compare LSVSR with earlier large-vocabulary visual speech datasets, including LRS3-TED.

entries.text: The authors claim LSVSR is an order of magnitude larger than any previous dataset, at 3,886 hours.
entries.condition: Authors' comparison of LSVSR with prior visual speech datasets.

entries.text: The pipeline starts from 140,000 hours of YouTube audio segments.
entries.condition: Segments were preselected from public YouTube videos and then passed through the paper's data pipeline.

entries.text: About 2% of the preselected YouTube clips satisfy the paper's filtering criteria.
entries.condition: The pipeline processes clips preselected from YouTube and applies the filters described in Section 3.

entries.text: Video sequences are represented as 128×128 frames stacked over time.
entries.condition: LSVSR video representation before V2P recognition.

entries.text: The clip-quality filter removes blurry clips and faces with eye-to-eye width below 80 pixels.
entries.condition: LSVSR video preprocessing.

entries.text: The pipeline discards videos below 23 fps.
entries.condition: LSVSR video preprocessing.

entries.text: Input videos above 30 fps are downsampled.
entries.condition: LSVSR video preprocessing; higher frame rates are not kept at their original rate.

entries.text: LSVSR retains face segments only when yaw and pitch remain within ±30°.
entries.unit: degrees of face yaw and pitch
entries.condition: The training data and corresponding held-out LSVSR evaluation use this face-angle filtering.

entries.text: For evaluation, the pipeline removes utterances with fewer than 6 words.
entries.condition: Applies to LSVSR evaluation sets.

entries.text: Blurry videos are removed from validation and test sets using a variance-of-the-Laplacian threshold but retained in training as augmentation.
entries.condition: LSVSR partition-specific video quality treatment.

entries.text: Transcripts are language-filtered, forced-aligned with a multi-pronunciation lexicon, and mapped to a reduced X-SAMPA inventory of 40 phonemes plus silence.
entries.condition: YouTube-derived English utterances; forced alignment supplies the phoneme sequences paired with video.

entries.text: The paired phoneme sequences are produced by standard forced alignment using a lexicon with multiple pronunciations.
entries.condition: English transcript segments are aligned to the video clips for LSVSR supervision.

entries.text: The transcript pipeline uses a language classifier to remove non-English utterances.
entries.condition: YouTube transcript filtering for LSVSR; the paper cites CLD3.

entries.text: The final V2P-Sync audio-video alignment filter is reported at 81.2% accuracy.
entries.condition: Accuracy is for the final audio-video synchronization filter; the paper does not specify a separate held-out evaluation set or class composition.

entries.text: The V2P-Sync score is averaged over 100 equally spaced segments of each audio-video pair.
entries.condition: The averaging is described as improving synchronization-filter accuracy.

entries.text: The temporal aggregation module uses three bidirectional LSTMs with hidden state size 768.
entries.condition: The network maps video frames to framewise phoneme distributions and is trained with CTC.

entries.text: The V2P vision module has five 3D convolutional layers with 64, 128, 256, 512, and 512 filters.
entries.condition: The convolutions explicitly extract spatiotemporal features from mouth-region video.

entries.text: The V2P output layer has 41 phoneme labels plus the CTC blank class.
entries.condition: Framewise distribution output used for CTC phoneme recognition.

entries.text: The vision module's receptive field spans 11 frames, about 0.36–0.44 seconds.
entries.condition: V2P spatiotemporal vision front end; authors say this is roughly twice a typical phoneme duration.

entries.text: V2P training is distributed across 64 workers for batch size 128 and uses group normalization instead of batch normalization.
entries.condition: The paper attributes this setup to GPU memory limits and noisy/synchronization-expensive batch-normalization statistics.

entries.text: Memory limits allow only two batch elements per GPU.
entries.condition: This is the per-worker GPU capacity motivating distributed training.

entries.text: V2P uses group normalization, computing statistics within channel groups instead of using batch normalization.
entries.condition: The paper motivates this choice by cross-worker communication cost and noisy statistics with two examples per GPU.

entries.text: A duration curriculum grows from 2 to 12 seconds over 200,000 training steps.
entries.condition: Applied to V2P training to accelerate learning.

entries.text: Appendix E specifies Adam with learning rate 10⁻⁴, momenta 0.9 and 0.999, and epsilon 10⁻⁸.
entries.unit: learning rate; first momentum; second momentum; epsilon
entries.condition: V2P training uses Adam's default hyperparameters except for the stated learning rate.

entries.text: The default Adam settings listed are first/second momenta 0.9/0.999 and epsilon 10⁻⁸.
entries.condition: Appendix E V2P optimization settings.

entries.text: Training augmentation randomly mirrors videos horizontally and varies brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue.
entries.condition: Image-frame augmentation intended to improve invariance to filming conditions.

entries.text: Decoding composes CTC-collapse, phoneme-to-word lexicon, and word n-gram WFSTs, then searches for likely word sequences.
entries.condition: The decoder operates on V2P phoneme distributions and returns word sequences.
entries.quote: In our work we make use of a combination of three individual (weighted) FSTs, or WFSTs.

entries.text: The word LM is a Katz-backoff 5-gram with about 50 million n-grams and a vocabulary of about one million; V2P-NoLM instead uses a 100k-word dictionary weighted by smoothed training-data frequencies.
entries.value: 5-gram; about 50 million n-grams; about 1 million words; 100,000 words for NoLM
entries.condition: The 5-gram is used for every Table 1 model except V2P-NoLM; the paper says Hagen Soltau provided the LM but does not identify its text-training corpus.
entries.quote: In our case, we use a 5-gram model with Katz backoff with about 50 million n-grams and a vocabulary size of about one million.

entries.text: V2P-NoLM weights dictionary words by their smoothed frequencies in training data, as a unigram language model.
entries.condition: V2P-NoLM decoding ablation on the LSVSR evaluation.

entries.text: V2P-NoLM uses a dictionary of 100,000 words.
entries.condition: V2P-NoLM decoding ablation on the LSVSR evaluation.

entries.text: Except for V2P-NoLM, all Table 1 models use the same 5-gram word-level LM during decoding.
entries.condition: Applies to Table 1; V2P-NoLM uses the 100k-word unigram-frequency alternative.

entries.text: PER, CER, and WER are total edit distance divided by the total ground-truth sequence length; uncertainty is estimated by bootstrap sampling.
entries.condition: The Table 1 caption calls the displayed bootstrap estimates standard deviations; Sec. 5.1 describes them as standard errors.

entries.text: The LSVSR held-out test set is roughly 37 minutes long, with approximately 63,000 video frames and 7,100 words.
entries.condition: Main V2P evaluation set; validation/test blurry videos were removed and utterances under 6 words were removed.

entries.text: The Table 1 caption calls the ± intervals bootstrap standard deviations; Sec. 5.1 refers to estimated standard errors.
entries.condition: The reported intervals are bootstrap-based and are not described as variation across independent training runs.

entries.text: Professional readers transcribed 153 videos with context and 274 without context.
entries.unit: videos, with context; videos, without context
entries.condition: Subsets of the LSVSR held-out test set used in the professional lipreader comparison.

entries.text: Professional readers could view each clip up to 10 times at half or normal speed.
entries.condition: Human evaluation protocol on modified whole-head crops of LSVSR test videos.

entries.text: For the with-context human subset, clips have at least 12 words and readers receive the first 6 words, title, and video category before transcribing the remainder.
entries.unit: minimum words per clip; preceding words provided
entries.condition: Human evaluation subset on the held-out LSVSR test set.

entries.text: Professional readers saw modified whole-head clips, whereas the model receives mouth-region video.
entries.condition: The human comparison uses held-out LSVSR test videos and differs from the model input crop.

entries.text: Professional lipreaders without context: WER 92.9±0.9% on 274 LSVSR test videos.
entries.condition: Subset of held-out LSVSR test; transcripts have at least 6 words; readers see whole-head video, may replay up to 10 times at half or normal speed, and receive no transcript/title/category context.

entries.text: Professional lipreaders with context: WER 86.4±1.4% on 153 LSVSR test videos.
entries.condition: Subset of held-out LSVSR test with at least 12 words; readers see whole-head video and are given the first 6 words, title, and video category before transcribing the remainder; replay up to 10 times at half or normal speed.

entries.text: Audio-Ph (58M parameters) scores PER 12.5±0.5%, CER 11.5±0.6%, and WER 18.3±0.9%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test (~37 min, ~63,000 frames, ~7,100 words; evaluation excludes <6-word clips and blurry validation/test clips); audio-only Deep Speech 2-based phoneme model; shared 5-gram word LM; mouth-region video conditions apply to the corpus, not the audio input.

entries.text: Audio-Ph is a Deep Speech 2-based ASR model trained to predict phonemes rather than characters, using audio instead of video.
entries.condition: The Audio-Ph comparison is an approximate audio-based performance bound on the LSVSR test utterances.

entries.text: Baseline-LipNet-Ch (7M parameters) scores CER 64.6±0.5% and WER 93.0±0.6%; PER is not reported.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering and shared 5-gram word LM; character-level CTC, FST decoding, and character lexicon.

entries.text: Baseline-LipNet-Ph (7M parameters) scores PER 65.8±0.4%, CER 72.8±0.5%, and WER 89.8±0.5%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering and shared 5-gram word LM; LipNet predicts phonemes with CTC and uses the same FST decoding pipeline.

entries.text: Baseline-Seq2seq-Ch (15M parameters) scores CER 49.9±0.6% and WER 76.8±0.8%; PER is not reported.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering; WAS-style character sequence-to-sequence model with the V2P 3D visual network substituted for its pretrained AV-sync network; shared 5-gram LM used for reranking.

entries.text: Baseline-LipNet-Large-Ph (40M parameters) scores PER 53.0±0.5%, CER 54.0±0.8%, and WER 72.7±1.0%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering and shared 5-gram word LM; size-matched V2P replica using GRUs, dropout, and no normalization.

entries.text: V2P-FullyConv (29M parameters) scores PER 41.3±0.6%, CER 36.7±0.9%, and WER 51.6±1.2%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering and shared 5-gram word LM; V2P temporal LSTMs are replaced by 6 dilated temporal-convolution layers with kernel 3 and dilation rates [1,1,2,4,8,16].

entries.text: V2P-NoLM (49M parameters) scores PER 33.6±0.6%, CER 34.6±0.8%, and WER 53.6±1.0%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test with the same evaluation filtering; during decoding the 5-gram LM is replaced with a 100k-word dictionary weighted by smoothed training-data unigram frequencies.

entries.text: V2P (49M parameters) scores PER 33.6±0.6%, CER 28.3±0.9%, and WER 40.9±1.2%.
entries.condition: Held-out LSVSR test (~37 min, ~63,000 frames, ~7,100 words; evaluation excludes <6-word clips and blurry validation/test clips); mouth-region video from the LSVSR ±30° yaw/pitch pipeline; shared Katz-backoff 5-gram word LM; ± values are bootstrap estimates.

entries.text: The authors claim the full V2P model nearly halves WER relative to the prior methods evaluated on LSVSR and performs best among their tested configurations.
entries.condition: Comparison is on the held-out LSVSR test set in Table 1; the authors specifically compare against their reproduced LipNet and WAS-style variants.

entries.text: The authors say removing the word LM raises V2P WER by approximately 13 absolute points, from 40.9% to 53.6%.
entries.condition: V2P vs V2P-NoLM on the same LSVSR test set; NoLM uses the 100k-word frequency-weighted dictionary.

entries.text: TM-seq2seq is listed at 57.9% WER on the full LRS3-TED test set; no filtered-test score is listed.
entries.condition: Externally reported TM-seq2seq result on full LRS3-TED test; the table gives no uncertainty estimate and no filtered-test result.

entries.text: Without LRS3-TED training or fine-tuning, V2P scores 47.0±1.6% WER on the filtered LRS3-TED test subset.
entries.condition: Zero-shot V2P evaluation on LRS3-TED; filtered test removes instances with larger face angles and clips shorter than the LSVSR filtering protocol; compared with the paper's TM-seq2seq result, for which Table 2 has no filtered score.

entries.text: Without LRS3-TED training or fine-tuning, V2P scores 55.1±0.9% WER on the full, unfiltered LRS3-TED test set.
entries.condition: Zero-shot evaluation on full LRS3-TED test, which includes faces up to ±90° and clips shorter than one second; Table 2 compares against TM-seq2seq's externally reported 57.9% without giving uncertainty for that baseline.

entries.text: LRS3-TED includes faces at angles up to ±90° and clips shorter than one second.
entries.condition: The full LRS3-TED test includes these conditions; the filtered subset removes larger face angles and shorter clips.

entries.text: The authors claim zero-shot generalization to LRS3-TED and state-of-the-art performance under different dataset conditions.
entries.condition: V2P was trained on LSVSR and not trained or fine-tuned on LRS3-TED; the full-test comparison is against TM-seq2seq.

entries.text: The cited Afouras et al. LRS3-TED work reports 57.9% WER for seq2seq and 61.8% for CTC.
entries.condition: Prior results on LRS3-TED from Afouras et al. (2018a); the paper describes those models as using pre-learned features.

entries.text: LipNet is reported at 4.8% WER with overlapping speakers and 11.4% with unseen speakers on GRID.
entries.condition: Prior LipNet results on GRID, a limited-grammar 51-word-vocabulary corpus with 28 hours of five-word sentences; the figures are overlapping-speaker and unseen-speaker evaluations respectively.

entries.text: Competent human lipreaders are reported at 47.7% WER on GRID.
entries.condition: Prior human result on GRID, whose grammar and vocabulary are limited; the paper does not give further reader or protocol details here.

entries.text: The cited WLAS system reports 50.2% WER on LRS, with professional lipreaders at 87.6% WER.
entries.condition: Prior results on LRS, an approximately 246-hour BBC-news dataset; the paper reports these as Chung et al. (2017) results.

entries.text: Cited multi-view lipreading results are 62.8% WER for profile views and 56.4% for frontal views.
entries.condition: Prior Chung and Zisserman (2017) multi-view sentence-level lipreading results; profile and frontal views respectively.

entries.text: Training seeds, repeated-run counts, and run-to-run variability are not reported; the displayed uncertainty comes from bootstrap sampling of evaluation rates.

entries.text: WER/CER/PER are normalized by reference sequence length, but text tokenization, case/punctuation normalization, and other scoring-normalization rules are not specified.

questions.q: What are the paper's main component-level contributions and the conditions on which they depend?
questions.answer: The authors combine a phoneme-predicting V2P network with WFST word decoding and claim vocabulary changes without network retraining (t1–t3, t10, t13–t14); LSVSR scale, labels, alignment, and video filtering are documented in t4–t9 and t8b–t8c.

questions.q: What exact results support the claimed LSVSR superiority, and what are their test conditions?
questions.answer: Table 1 gives per-model PER/CER/WER and parameter counts with the LSVSR test and comparison conditions in t16–t25; the authors' near-halving claim is t26 and the LM ablation is t27.

questions.q: How strong is the external LRS3-TED generalization evidence?
questions.answer: The paper reports zero-shot V2P WER on filtered and full LRS3-TED (t28–t31), cites prior LRS3 scores in t32, and the filtered TM-seq2seq comparator is absent from Table 2 (u11).

questions.q: Which evaluation conditions remain unresolved for a component review?
questions.answer: The paper omits split/speaker overlap, seeds, validation-selection details, input and text normalization, decoding and LM selection settings, chance level, LRS3 counts, and V2P-Sync test protocol (u1–u11, u13).

questions.q: What author-conceded limitations matter for deployment or interpreting comparisons?
questions.answer: The authors restrict effective operation to particular camera/view and quality conditions, say the speaking filter misses voice-overs, describe medical use as potential, disclose the WAS baseline substitution, and report angle-range robustness (t42–t46).

questions.q: Writer check: does the target cite Sanabria et al. 2016 or Thangthai & Harvey 2017, and where does it credit earlier deep-network + HMM lipreading?
questions.answer: Neither is in the reference list; Sec. 2 credits 'combining deep networks with traditional speech techniques (e.g. HMMs and GMM-HMMs)' to Noda 2014, Koller 2015, Almajai 2016, Takashima 2016, and cites Eesen for the WFST recipe.
